The use of the VR headset in Experiment 3 of the study is primarily tied to the experimental design's goal of distinguishing between two competing hypotheses about the nature of bimanual haptic slant adaptation. Specifically, the researchers aimed to determine whether the adaptation was based on **relative static posture between the hands** (i.e., a bimanual stage involving intermanual comparison) or on **low-level unimanual adaptation** (i.e., individual hand postures being adapted independently). 

The VR environment allowed for precise control over **hand positions in 3D space** without requiring a physical surface or haptic feedback—something that was crucial for testing the **posture-based** aspect of adaptation. By rendering a virtual environment, the researchers could manipulate the **relative positions** of the hands independently and test how adaptation effects changed when testing at different heights. This setup enabled them to investigate **whether posture alone** (through proprioception) or **haptic feedback** (through a physical surface) was necessary for the observed aftereffects.

The VR headset also facilitated **participant guidance and measurement** of hand positions in a controlled and consistent manner, even in the absence of an actual haptic surface. This is particularly important for isolating the role of posture and examining whether adaptation occurred at the level of **individual hand settings** (unimanual) or **intermanual comparisons** (bimanual).

While the study did conclude that haptic feedback is unnecessary (as supported by the results of the Surface Absent condition), the **reason for using VR** in this specific experiment was to **explore the distinction between relative posture and unimanual adaptation**, rather than to prove the redundancy of haptic feedback. The VR setup provided a flexible environment to test these conditions while minimizing the influence of haptic cues, enabling a clearer assessment of the **proprioceptive basis** of the adaptation.

Thus, the VR headset was used to **distinguish between an effect due to relative static posture** (bimanual) and **unimanual adaptation**.
